chunks: From him (Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl) from Ibn Mahbub from Malik ibn Atiyyah from Sawrah ibn Kulaib, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who divorced his wife with a single revocable divorce while she was in a state of purity, without sexual intercourse, with witnesses, the divorce of the Sunnah. She was one who menstruates. Three months passed and she did not menstruate except for one period, then her menstruation ceased, so another three months passed and she did not know what had stopped her menstruation. He (peace be upon him) said: If she is a young woman with regular menstruation, and she does not menstruate in three months except for one period, then her menstruation ceases and she does not know what stopped it, then she waits (for the waiting period) for nine months from the day he divorced her. Then she observes her waiting period after that for three months, then she may marry if she wishes.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: This report should be acted upon because she is cleared of pregnancy by nine months, which is the maximum duration of pregnancy, so it is known that she is not pregnant. Then she observes her waiting period after that, which is three months. And we interpret the first report as a case of supererogatory precaution, that she observes the waiting period until fifteen months.
ai.seo_question: What is the waiting period for a divorced woman whose menstruation stops or becomes irregular?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-istibsar elucidates the complex jurisprudence of 'Iddah for a woman experiencing irregular menstruation (Haid al-Nisa') after a single revocable divorce. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) prescribes a nine-month period of Istibra to confirm the absence of pregnancy, followed by a three-month waiting period, a ruling that Muhammad ibn al-Hasan validates as the primary operational standard due to its alignment with the maximum gestation period. The text also acknowledges a secondary, more precautionary view extending the total waiting period to fifteen months, reflecting the scholarly tradition of balancing definitive legal certainty with prudent caution.
